# FalconHTTP v1.0.0

The first stable release of **FalconHTTP**, an embedded C++ HTTP server library built on this project's own container, caching, concurrency, JSON, and function-wrapper libraries.

## Highlights

- Full HTTP/1.1 request/response model: `HttpRequest`/`HttpResponse` with case-insensitive header handling (RFC 7230-compliant), query and path parameters, and JSON body helpers.
- `HttpParser`/`HttpSerializer`: parses a complete raw request buffer into an `HttpRequest`, serializes an `HttpResponse` back to wire-format bytes.
- `Router`: pattern-based routing with `:param` path segments via `PathMatcher`, method-aware dispatch that distinguishes `NotFound` (404) from `MethodNotAllowed` (405) rather than collapsing both into a generic miss.
- Onion-model middleware chain (`Server::use()`), with built-in `Cors`, `Logger`, and `Recovery` middleware — the latter converting any uncaught exception into a clean 500 instead of taking down the handling thread.
- `StaticFileServer` backed by an LRU `FileCache`, with path-traversal protection and MIME-type resolution via `MimeTypes`.
- Thread-pool-backed `Server`, configurable end-to-end via `ServerConfig` (port, thread count, and DoS-protection caps).
- Request-size DoS protections: `maxHeaderSize`/`maxBodySize` caps returning 431/413 before an oversized request is ever fully buffered.
- Move-only `Socket`/`Connection`/`Listener` — no accidental duplication of a native OS handle.
- Built directly on `FunctionPro`, `HashMapPro`, `JsonParser`, `LRUCache`, `ThreadPoolPro`, and `VectorPro`.

## Performance

The request-handling path is designed around avoiding unnecessary allocation, redundant work, and repeated computation:

- Header names are normalized to lowercase once, on insert — lookups compare directly rather than re-normalizing on every `hasHeader()`/`header()` call.
- `HttpSerializer` computes `Content-Length` and `Connection` directly from the response at serialization time, rather than buffering first and measuring after.
- The LRU-backed `FileCache` avoids re-reading and re-resolving the same static file from disk on every repeated request.
- `Server`'s thread pool is constructed once per process and reused across every accepted connection, rather than spawning an OS thread per request.
- The middleware chain is a straightforward recursive call, not a per-request heap-allocated queue — chain overhead is bounded by the number of middleware actually registered.

## Benchmarks

Unlike `LRUCache`, FalconHTTP has no natural drop-in standard-library
equivalent to benchmark against (there's no `std::` HTTP parser, router,
or serializer) — these are absolute measurements, not a comparison.
Figures below are at 1M iterations; full results across every
subsystem and scale: `benchmarks/results/v1_0_0.md`.

| Test                                       | 1M       |
|---------------------------------------------|----------|
| FileCache::get() Existing Entry              | 33.97 ms |
| FileCache::put() Fresh Key                   | 169.04 ms|
| Router::dispatch() Matching Route            | 520.17 ms|
| Router::dispatch() No Matching Route         | 241.79 ms|
| Parse() 50 Headers                           | 5.45 s   |
| Serialize() 50 Headers                       | 650.93 ms|
| 3-middleware Chain + Handler                 | 124.52 ms|
| Dispatch() Last Of 2000 Routes                | 41.93 s  |
| Connection Create + Move Construction        | 2.35 s   |

A few things worth calling out honestly:

- **`Router::dispatch()`'s linear-scan cost is real and now quantified.**
  Going from a 10-route table to a 2000-route table makes dispatching
  to the last-registered route roughly **~142x slower** (295.91 ms vs
  41.93 s at 1M) — a 200x increase in route count producing a
  near-proportional increase in cost, exactly what an unindexed linear
  scan predicts. This was flagged as an architectural concern during
  review; it isn't a problem for small route tables, but it's the
  clearest case for prioritizing a trie/radix-based `Router` before
  this library is used with a large number of routes.
- **Parsing 50 headers costs ~8.4x more than serializing the same 50**
  (5.45 s vs 650.93 ms at 1M). The asymmetry is worth investigating —
  `HttpParser` allocates a new lowercase-normalized `std::string` per
  header on insert (`HttpRequest::setHeader()`'s case normalization),
  does a line-by-line split and trim, and inserts into a `HashMap`,
  while `HttpSerializer` just iterates already-normalized entries and
  appends to one output buffer. The per-header marginal cost in the
  Scaling suite's growth data also *increases* with header count
  (roughly 48 ns/header at 5 headers vs 128 ns/header at 500), which
  looks like `HashMap` rehashing overhead compounding rather than pure
  O(n) parsing cost — worth profiling before assuming this is as fast
  as it can go.
- **`Connection`'s move construction is effectively free.** Create +
  move (2.35 s at 1M) is statistically indistinguishable from plain
  `Socket::createTcp()` + `close()` alone (also 2.35 s at 1M) —
  confirming the caveat noted in that benchmark's own comments: the
  move itself adds no measurable cost on top of socket creation.
- **`Server` construction is fast enough to suggest `ThreadMarket`
  reuse is actually working.** ~11.9 μs per construct+destruct with 4
  threads (11.88 s / 1M) is only ~5x the cost of a single
  `Socket::createTcp()` + `close()` pair (2.35 μs) — far cheaper than
  4 real OS thread spawn/joins would cost if that were happening on
  every construction. This resolves the uncertainty flagged in
  `server_construction.cpp`'s own comments.

## Testing

The project includes a comprehensive test suite covering:

- Unit-level correctness for `HttpMethod`, `HttpStatus`, `MimeTypes`, `UrlDecoder`, `PathMatcher`, `HttpRequest`, `HttpResponse`, `HttpSerializer`, `Socket` options, and `Router` registration/dispatch, in isolation
- Cross-component integration: the full parse → dispatch → serialize pipeline, middleware chain composition and short-circuiting, CORS preflight handling, static file serving round trips, and route parameter extraction driven through the real parser rather than constructed by hand
- Regression coverage pinning every bug fixed during development (request body truncation from a header-offset miscalculation, a socket-send error silently reported as success, header lookup case-insensitivity, oversized-header/body rejection, `405 Method Not Allowed` reachability, `Connection: close` on every response, and duplicate `Content-Length`/`Connection` header emission) so none of them can silently return
- Lifecycle correctness: move-only `Socket`/`Connection` RAII, `Listener` bind/close cycles, and `Server` start/run/stop state transitions
- Concurrency correctness: thread-safe `Logger`/`Recovery` output under the shared thread pool, concurrent `FileCache` access, and concurrent `Router::dispatch()` with no cross-request state leakage

## Code Coverage

The current test suite achieves:

- **92.8% line coverage** (643 / 693 lines)
- **96.6% function coverage** (114 / 118 functions)

| Directory    | Line Coverage    | Function Coverage |
|--------------|------------------|--------------------|
| `Core`       | 90.3% (205/227)  | 94.6% (35/37)      |
| `FileServer` | 96.7% (58/60)    | 100.0% (8/8)       |
| `HTTP`       | 92.2% (249/270)  | 95.5% (42/44)      |
| `Middleware` | 91.1% (41/45)    | 100.0% (8/8)       |
| `Routing`    | 100.0% (54/54)   | 100.0% (8/8)       |
| `Utility`    | 96.2% (25/26)    | 100.0% (2/2)       |

`Core` is the softest spot of the six — both its line coverage (90.3%)
and function coverage (94.6%) are the lowest in the table, worth a
look before the next release to see which paths (likely error/edge
cases in `Server`, `Socket`, `Listener`, or `Connection`) aren't
exercised yet.

## Continuous Integration

Automated builds and packaging checks are configured across:

- Conan and vcpkg packaging, each verified with a real consumer smoke test (`test_package.cpp` / `smoke_test.cpp`) against the built package

*(The rest of the CI matrix — compilers, sanitizer jobs, static-analysis/formatting checks, and coverage collection — should be filled in and verified against the project's actual CI configuration before publishing, rather than assumed from MiniDB's setup. Noting here so nothing is asserted without confirmation.)*

## Release

This release represents the first stable version of FalconHTTP and establishes its initial HTTP request/response model, routing, middleware, static file serving, and thread-pool-backed server, along with its cross-platform build and packaging pipeline.

## Installation

Clone the repository and integrate FalconHTTP into your C++ project using the provided CMake configuration.

See the project documentation for build instructions, API usage, and integration details.
